title: Univariate descriptive analysis
question: What does one variable look like?
what: Summarizes a variable's distribution: counts and percentages for categories; center, spread and range for numbers.
use: Start here to inspect missing values, unusual values, skew and group sizes before fitting a model.
data: One categorical or numeric variable; each row represents a case.
read: Use the mean and SD for center and spread; compare the median and quartiles when values are skewed. Charts reveal patterns a single average misses.
caution: Describing a sample does not establish a relationship or a causal effect. Check which rows and weights are active.
example: Describe respondents' ages or the percentage in each party.

title: Welch independent-samples t-test
question: Do two independent groups have different means?
what: Tests a difference between two group means without assuming equal variances.
use: Compare different cases in two groups.
data: One numeric outcome and a group variable; select two groups.
read: The difference is first group minus second. Read its confidence interval and two-sided p-value.
caution: Cases must be independent. This calculator's classical t-tests require unweighted data.
example: Compare average income in treatment and control groups.

title: One-sample t-test
question: Does a mean differ from a reference value?
what: Tests whether a population mean differs from a specified number.
use: Compare a sample with a target or scale midpoint.
data: One numeric outcome and a reference value.
read: Read the estimated mean, difference from the reference, confidence interval and two-sided p-value.
caution: Use independent, unweighted observations. Strong outliers or very small skewed samples can make inference unreliable.
example: Compare average satisfaction with the midpoint of 3.
aliases: one sample t test reference midpoint

title: Paired-samples t-test
question: Did the same cases change between two measurements?
what: Tests whether the mean within-case difference is zero.
use: Compare matched observations, such as before and after.
data: Two numeric columns, with each pair on the same row.
read: The difference is first measurement minus second; inspect its confidence interval and p-value.
caution: This is not a test for unrelated groups. Incomplete pairs are excluded; differences should not be dominated by outliers. Use unweighted data here.
example: Compare the same students' pre- and post-course scores.
aliases: paired t test before after matched

title: One-way ANOVA
question: Do means differ across several independent groups?
what: Tests the null hypothesis that all group population means are equal.
use: Compare a numeric outcome across three or more groups defined by one categorical variable.
data: One numeric outcome and one group variable; independent cases.
read: The F-test indicates whether at least one mean differs. The group table shows which differences deserve further investigation.
caution: The classical F-test assumes a common within-group variance. A significant result does not identify the differing pairs; the calculator does not automatically run post-hoc comparisons. Two groups route to a t-test.
example: Compare average scores across three teaching methods.

title: Chi-square test of independence
question: Are two categorical variables associated?
what: Compares observed table counts with counts expected if the variables were independent.
use: Examine whether the distribution of one category variable varies across another.
data: Two categorical variables recorded for the same cases.
read: Read the chi-square p-value together with percentages and Cramér's V, which describes association strength.
caution: Independent cases and adequate expected cell counts matter. Sparse tables can give unreliable approximations. The test does not establish causation; weighted tables here are not a full survey-adjusted chi-square test.
example: Compare party preference across regions.

title: Pearson correlation
question: How strongly do two numeric variables follow a straight-line pattern?
what: Measures linear association on a scale from -1 to +1.
use: Describe the direction and strength of a relationship between two numeric variables.
data: Two numeric variables on the same rows; the calculation uses valid pairs.
read: The sign gives direction and the magnitude gives linear strength. Inspect the scatterplot alongside r and its p-value.
caution: Outliers and curved relationships can mislead. Correlation does not prove causation. Repeated measurements need an analysis that handles dependence.
example: Examine the association between study hours and exam scores.

title: Spearman rank correlation
question: Do higher values of one variable tend to accompany higher or lower values of another?
what: Measures association between ranks rather than the original numerical distances.
use: Explore an ordered, monotonic relationship that need not be a straight line.
data: Two ordered variables, stored numerically; meaningful ordering is required.
read: The sign and magnitude of rho describe the ranked relationship. Correlation displays Pearson and Spearman together.
caution: It does not detect every nonlinear pattern and does not solve dependence or confounding. P-values with ties or small samples are approximate here.
example: Relate respondents' ordered rankings of two priorities.

title: OLS linear regression
question: How does a numeric outcome relate to several predictors?
what: Fits an additive model for the conditional mean of a numeric outcome by minimizing squared residuals.
use: Estimate adjusted associations, compare groups while accounting for other variables, or calculate fitted values.
data: A numeric outcome and numeric or categorical predictors, with one row per case.
read: A coefficient is the outcome-unit difference for a one-unit predictor change, holding included predictors constant; categorical effects compare with a reference group.
caution: Check functional form, outliers and residual dependence. Robust or clustered errors change uncertainty, not confounding. An observational coefficient is not automatically causal.
example: Relate income to education, experience and region.

title: Binary logistic regression
question: What predicts a yes/no outcome?
what: Models the log odds of an event and produces fitted probabilities between zero and one.
use: Study a binary outcome while adjusting for other predictors.
data: An outcome with two categories and numeric or categorical predictors. Check which category is modeled as the event.
read: A coefficient is a log-odds change; exponentiating it gives an odds ratio. An odds ratio is not a probability change or a risk ratio.
caution: Sparse categories or perfect prediction can prevent convergence. Check dependence, sample size and uncertainty before interpreting effects.
example: Model whether a respondent voted using age, education and interest.

title: Ordinal logistic regression
question: What predicts an outcome with ordered categories?
what: Fits a proportional-odds model for the cumulative ordering of outcome categories.
use: Study outcomes such as low, medium and high without treating category spacing as equal.
data: Ordered categories stored as numeric codes and one or more predictors. The numerical order must match the intended order.
read: Positive coefficients favor higher categories in this implementation. Thresholds separate cumulative categories; predicted probabilities describe each category.
caution: The proportional-odds assumption requires common predictor effects across cutpoints. It is unsuitable for unordered categories and is not a multilevel model.
example: Relate a five-level satisfaction response to service use and age.

title: Poisson count regression
question: What predicts how many events occur?
what: Uses a log link to model the expected number of events as a positive quantity.
use: Relate event counts to predictors when cases have comparable exposure.
data: A nonnegative integer count outcome and one or more predictors.
read: Exponentiating a coefficient gives a multiplicative ratio of expected counts, holding other predictors constant.
caution: Check overdispersion and excess zeros. This screen has no exposure-offset field, so unequal observation times or populations need additional modeling. Do not enter a continuous rate as if it were an integer count.
example: Model complaint counts per office over equal observation periods.

sources.label: R: Poisson family and log link

title: Word frequencies and word cloud
question: Which words appear most often in a collection of texts?
what: Counts retained words across documents after the selected text-cleaning rules.
use: Explore vocabulary, recurring terms and candidate dictionary keywords.
data: A text column with one document per row.
read: A token count is the number of occurrences; document frequency is the number of texts containing the word. The cloud is a visual summary.
caution: Common words are not necessarily important concepts. Stopwords, minimum word length, language and document length affect counts; these tools do not automatically infer sentiment or topics.
example: Explore the most common words in open-ended survey responses.

title: Keywords in context (KWIC)
question: How is a particular word used?
what: Displays matching words with surrounding text so their meaning can be inspected.
use: Check ambiguity, phrasing and whether a proposed keyword captures the intended concept.
data: A text column and a search term; click a word in the frequency table or enter a keyword.
read: Read the surrounding words and compare contexts across documents or groups.
caution: A keyword match alone does not identify agreement, negation, irony or a causal mechanism. Review examples before labeling a category.
example: Check whether 'school' refers to education policy or a person's biography.

title: Dictionary-based text analysis
question: How often do texts mention concepts defined by a list of keywords?
what: Matches words to user-defined categories and creates document-level counts or presence indicators.
use: Measure predefined themes transparently, then compare their prevalence or use generated variables in other analyses.
data: One document per row and a dictionary whose keywords match the texts' language and domain.
read: Counts measure matched mentions; a 0/1 indicator records any match. They are measurements defined by your dictionary, not direct measures of intent.
caution: Validate matches and missed meanings with manual reading. Polysemy, negation and longer documents can distort comparisons; a dictionary needs substantive justification.
example: Count education-related mentions using 'school', 'teacher' and 'tuition'.

title: Time trends and interrupted time series
question: Did an outcome's level or trend change around an event?
what: Fits a trend over ordered periods, optionally adding a level change, slope change, both, or a temporary pulse at an event.
use: Study regularly observed outcomes before and after a known intervention; the workspace also supports multiple units and prepared aggregate series.
data: A numeric outcome, a validated calendar/time variable and, for panels, a unit ID. Set event timing and transformations explicitly.
read: The pre-event trend describes change per period; event terms describe an immediate shift and/or a change in trend. AR(1) adjusts a specific form of residual autocorrelation.
caution: Check gaps, duplicates, seasonality and serial dependence. A simultaneous shock can explain an apparent event effect. This is not automatic forecasting or proof of a causal effect.
example: Examine monthly service use before and after a policy change.

sources.label: Bernal et al.: interrupted time series tutorial

aliases: ITS interrupted segmented time series trend AR1 panel

title: Network description and centrality
question: How is a network organized, and which nodes occupy distinctive positions?
what: Summarizes ties and computes node positions: degree counts ties; betweenness captures shortest-path brokerage; closeness/harmonic use distances; eigenvector/PageRank weight connections to other nodes.
use: Describe connectivity, compare node roles and choose informative plot sizes or layouts.
data: An edge list with two endpoint columns; an optional node list supplies IDs, attributes and isolates.
read: Choose the measure that matches the substantive meaning of importance. Direction and disconnected components affect results.
caution: Layout positions are visual arrangements, not estimated distances. Centrality does not demonstrate influence or causation; normalizations and unreachable-node conventions differ by measure.
example: Identify highly connected accounts or brokers between communities.

title: Network tie model (ERGM / MPLE)
question: Which attributes and network structures are associated with ties?
what: Models tie formation using an edge baseline plus terms such as reciprocity, shared partners, matching attributes and attribute differences.
use: Explore whether ties are associated with node characteristics or local network configurations.
data: A defined node set, edge list, correct directed/undirected setting and any required node attributes.
read: Coefficients describe conditional tie log odds for changes in model statistics, not ordinary independent-person regression effects.
caution: This calculator uses maximum pseudolikelihood. With reciprocity or triangles, displayed conditional standard errors do not fully handle network dependence; treat inference as exploratory and use full network estimation and diagnostics for substantive claims.
example: Explore whether organizations in the same sector are more likely to collaborate.
aliases: exponential random graph model pseudolikelihood MPLE

title: Confirmatory factor analysis (CFA)
question: Do selected items measure the proposed underlying concepts?
what: Specifies latent factors measured by observed items and evaluates how well the proposed measurement structure fits.
use: Assess a theory-defined measurement model before interpreting relationships between factors.
data: Several numeric indicators per factor; usually at least three. One loading per factor is fixed to set its scale.
read: Inspect loadings, item residuals and overall fit together. Standardized loadings describe the item-factor relationship on a common scale.
caution: This is confirmatory, not automatic factor discovery. Good fit does not prove validity. The calculator treats indicators as numeric/continuous; it does not provide a categorical-indicator estimator.
example: Model trust using several survey items intended to measure it.

title: Structural equation modeling (SEM)
question: How do measured latent concepts relate to one another?
what: Combines a factor measurement model with directional paths or correlations between factors.
use: Evaluate a proposed system of relationships while explicitly modeling item measurement error.
data: Identified factors with numeric indicators, justified paths and enough observations for stable estimation.
read: Read loadings, path coefficients, uncertainty and fit indices together. A path's direction is an assumption of the model, not a finding that proves causality.
caution: ML uses complete cases; the missing-data option uses full-information ML under appropriate missingness assumptions; ADF needs large samples. Rerun after edits. The current SEM fit ignores selected sampling weights.
example: Examine a proposed path from trust to engagement, with multiple items measuring each.

title: Scale reliability (Cronbach's alpha)
question: Do several items show internal consistency?
what: Summarizes item covariance relative to the variance of their combined scale.
use: Check internal consistency when multiple items are intended to measure one construct.
data: Several numeric items on the same rows, coded in a consistent direction. The calculation here uses complete cases.
read: Read alpha alongside item content, scale length and dimensionality; more items can increase alpha.
caution: A high alpha does not prove one factor, validity or absence of redundant items. Reverse-code negatively worded items before calculating it.
example: Check consistency among items in a proposed satisfaction scale.

title: Reading results: key terms
question: What do outcome, coefficient, p-value and confidence interval mean?
what: The outcome is what a model describes or predicts. Predictors are variables used to explain variation in it. A coefficient describes a model-specific association.
use: Distinguish effect size, uncertainty and substantive importance when reading output.
data: Check the analyzed N, missing rows, filters, reference groups and selected weights for every result.
read: A p-value measures incompatibility with a specified null model; it is not the probability the null is true. A 95% confidence procedure covers the target parameter in 95% of repeated samples under its assumptions.
caution: Statistical significance is not practical importance or causality. Standard errors quantify uncertainty; robust and clustered choices address particular error structures, not bias from omitted causes. Weighting does not automatically account for a complex survey design.
example: Report an estimated difference and its interval, then explain whether that difference matters in context.
aliases: p value confidence interval coefficient outcome predictor robust clustered weights standard error
